slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Putting Three ADSA Equity Goals into Practice
Connect three relevant ADSA equity goals with the conditions, responsibilities, and evidence that can support meaningful action.
Advanced self-directed learning
slides.narration: A goal names a direction; a useful work plan connects that direction with what people encounter in the actual work. This course helps supervisors and managers examine that connection while other staff can explore the reasoning as well. You will compare service and workforce examples, identify how goals can reinforce one another, and revise a proposal. The purpose is a practical plan with consultant guidance as needed, preserving actual responsibilities and distinguishing intended improvement from evidence of what has changed.

slides.text:
Start with the shared understanding
In the One DSD arrangement, the Equity Director briefs leadership on the six ADSA goals and answers their questions.

Supervisors and managers then use the work plan to select three goals and put them into practice, with the consultant providing consultation and guidance as needed.
slides.narration: This sequence reflects One DSD’s approach to putting the ADSA equity goals into practice. Leadership first has an opportunity to understand the six goals and ask questions. Supervisors and managers then develop their three-goal work plans, supported by the consultant. This does not create a new agency approval chain or replace existing responsibilities. It connects understanding with practical choices in each area. The consultant can help examine evidence, barriers, alternatives, and recommendations while the people responsible for the work carry out the decisions and actions within their roles.

slides.text:
The six goals in the program
Eliminating disparities; Community engagement; Hiring and retention.

Learning and development; Contracts and procurement; Communication and accessibility.

Select three relevant to the work, with reasons. The choice does not imply that the other goals are unimportant or that every course must address all six.
slides.narration: These are the six goal names recorded in the program requirements. They cover related aspects of service and workplace practice. Selecting three creates a focused plan, not permission to ignore another actual responsibility. The choice should be explained through the conditions the area needs to examine. A service question might connect communication with participation and contracting; a workforce question might connect opportunity with learning and retention. The connection must fit the facts rather than become three labels attached to an otherwise unchanged activity.

slides.text:
Worked example: three connected goals
Example question: people can read a service notice but cannot use the follow-up route.

Selected goals: Communication and accessibility; Community engagement; Contracts and procurement.

The plan examines the route, affected people’s accounts, and relevant provider expectations. Actual authority and a better result remain open.
slides.narration: The three goals connect around a particular condition. Communication concerns the usable explanation and route. Community engagement can help staff understand how the route is experienced while choices remain open. Contract questions may matter if a provider arrangement supplies part of the response, through the actual purchasing and service responsibilities. The practice example does not establish that a contract must change or that one remedy is feasible. It shows how the goals can guide a substantive inquiry instead of functioning as headings only.

slides.text:
Three goals attached to a notice
In this example, an area selects Communication and accessibility, Community engagement, and Contracts and procurement for a service notice with an unusable follow-up route. Which plan is most useful?
A. Examine the route, affected accounts, and provider expectations through actual roles; keep effects and unknowns visible.
B. Count three presentations and declare all three goals achieved.
C. Change a provider contract immediately because selecting the goal supplies authority.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The three goals fit a specific condition only when their connection is explained. Communication concerns the usable follow-up route. Engagement can bring affected accounts into an open comparison. A contract question may matter if an actual provider arrangement supplies the response, but that relationship still needs examination. The plan should preserve actual authority and seek consultant analysis where useful. Repeated use of goal labels without a work connection can leave the same gate unchanged. The practice case supplies no approved contract change or result; it offers a question and alternatives that need the appropriate responsibilities and evidence.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Examine the route, affected accounts, and provider expectations through actual roles; keep effects and unknowns visible.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Count three presentations and declare all three goals achieved.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Change a provider contract immediately because selecting the goal supplies authority.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This connects each goal to the condition. A recurring route gate may limit clarification. Compare alternatives through actual roles and examine use; a contract change, approved remedy, and improved outcome are not established.

What does each selected goal contribute to the same service question?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: This response explains why each goal belongs in the plan and keeps the inquiry grounded in an actual condition. The route may repeatedly limit clarification, but its extent and effects need examination. Appropriate colleagues and consultant guidance can help compare alternatives. Selecting a goal does not authorize a contract change or establish that a proposed remedy is feasible or effective.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Presentations may support learning but do not resolve the route by themselves. Repetition can leave a barrier behind goal labels. Connect learning with the actual condition and evidence; goal achievement remains unestablished.

What does each selected goal contribute to the same service question?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Learning activities can contribute to understanding while the route remains unusable. Counting them as complete achievement of three goals changes an activity account into an unsupported outcome. Repetition can make the plan look finished without examining the gate. Connect the learning with the condition, actual responsibilities, and evidence about use. None of the goals is shown achieved merely by presentation counts.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A selected goal does not create contracting authority. Repetition of that shortcut can obscure required review and actual effects. Examine the relevant arrangement with responsible colleagues; no contract change is authorized by the exercise.

What does each selected goal contribute to the same service question?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The plan names a relevant question; it does not supply independent contracting authority. An immediate change without the actual process could create another problem or miss the relevant arrangement. Bring the supported concern and alternatives to responsible colleagues, with consultant analysis as useful. The exercise authorizes no contract decision and establishes neither feasibility nor an improved service result.

slides.text:
Find the work before adding another process
An existing service review, learning arrangement, or workforce practice may already address part of the goal. Examine it before proposing a duplicate.

A missing work-plan row does not establish that equity work is absent. Identify what is actually done and where a supported gap remains.
slides.narration: A work plan should help the work become clear, not require every useful practice to be rebuilt in a new form. Ask which existing arrangements already support the selected goals and what evidence is available about their use. A separate plan, an established procedure, or a daily practice can all be relevant. Repeatedly adding new activity without examining existing work may create burden while leaving the real condition untouched. The next proposal should respond to a supported gap, not simply a blank field.

slides.text:
Describe the condition and possible mechanism
State what people encounter and how a routine may repeatedly shape access, opportunity, or burden. Keep observations and explanations distinct.

A usable plan asks about a specific mechanism. It does not assume that every difference proves discrimination or that one activity eliminates disparities.
slides.narration: The mechanism connects an action or arrangement with a possible effect. For example, a follow-up route available through only one method may restrict clarification for some people. Repetition can make that gate part of ordinary service practice. The effect still needs examination in actual use. A workforce example might follow how early preparation affects later assignment evidence. Describe the condition carefully, name the possible connection, and keep unknowns visible rather than treating a broad goal as a finding about cause.

slides.text:
Ask why these three belong together
Explain what each selected goal contributes to the question and where their actions may reinforce or complicate one another.

Do not assume that more activity means more progress. A change supporting one goal may create a burden relevant to another.
slides.narration: A communication improvement may require staff preparation, and that learning may need usable formats or support within the work. A contracting change might improve response expectations while increasing a burden that smaller providers find difficult to meet. These are questions to examine, not reasons to avoid the goals. A useful plan brings the connections into the comparison. That makes the intended direction clearer and helps the responsible people consider alternatives rather than treating each goal as an isolated activity count.

slides.text:
Community knowledge before choices close
Invite relevant perspectives to examine the condition and alternatives while the decision can still be informed. Explain the available influence and actual limits.

A contribution does not imply endorsement or representation of a whole community. Use the account to improve the question, not decorate a finished plan.
slides.narration: A person may explain that the notice is clear but the contact route is not, or that the route works while the response does not answer the consequential question. Those differences can change what the plan needs to examine. Engagement is more useful when that knowledge reaches an open choice. Explain how contributions will be considered and preserve permissions and privacy. Repeated late invitations can leave the same condition outside the design while making participation appear complete in a report.

slides.text:
Compare feasible responses
Compare the current approach and practical alternatives for relevant access, benefit, burden, resources, and actual requirements.

Seek consultant analysis and guidance where helpful. A proposal should name its uncertainty rather than claim an effect that has not been examined.
slides.narration: The consultant can contribute substantive research and equity analysis alongside the people who know the work. That collaboration can help identify a missing perspective, compare an alternative, or clarify an assumption. It does not transfer every decision to the consultant or create a mandatory review gate for ordinary resource use. Keep the comparison grounded in actual facts and responsibilities. A proposed response may be worth pursuing while its costs, feasibility, and eventual effects remain questions that the plan must not hide.

slides.text:
A workforce plan built around the same circle
In this example, an area selects Hiring and retention, Learning and development, and Eliminating disparities. Only staff already familiar with the manager receive preparation for development assignments. What should the plan examine?
A. The manager’s friends as proof of misconduct.
B. A universal requirement that everyone accept the same assignment.
C. Examine information, preparation, support, and task criteria across the route, preserving actual processes and staff choice.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The selected workforce goals can connect through a practical opportunity path. The case identifies preparation available through familiarity, which may shape later evidence of readiness. That possible mechanism deserves inquiry without policing private friendships or declaring misconduct. Compare information, support, criteria, and actual employee choice across the relevant stages. Consultant guidance can help examine the pattern and alternatives, while employment responsibilities remain with the proper roles. Repeated narrow preparation routes may carry opportunity forward to the same circle. The case supplies no complete cause, individual motive, formal finding, or proof that one alternative will resolve the gap.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. The manager’s friends as proof of misconduct.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. A universal requirement that everyone accept the same assignment.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Examine information, preparation, support, and task criteria across the route, preserving actual processes and staff choice.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The relationship pattern does not establish misconduct. Repeated personal accusations can distract from the opportunity gate. Examine information, support, and criteria through actual roles; motive and formal findings remain unknown.

Where could earlier preparation shape the evidence used for a later opportunity?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Private relationships alone do not establish wrongdoing. The useful inquiry concerns whether essential preparation is available through a legitimate route and how relevant criteria are applied. Repeated focus on personal accusations can obscure that condition. Preserve actual employment processes and evidence responsibilities. The case supplies no finding about motive, capability, discrimination, or the appropriate individual outcome.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Equal obligation is not the same as usable opportunity. Repetition can burden staff with different goals or conditions. Examine legitimate access and support while preserving choice; an identical assignment is not established as the remedy.

Where could earlier preparation shape the evidence used for a later opportunity?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: Making everyone accept the same assignment would replace an access question with a compulsory career path. Staff can have different goals and practical conditions. Repetition of identical demands may create another burden. Examine usable information, preparation, and support through actual responsibilities, while preserving choice and genuine work requirements. No universal assignment or equal result is established by the exercise.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This connects the goals with a repeatable preparation gate. Prior access may become later readiness evidence. Compare usable routes and actual criteria, with guidance where helpful; individual motives, selection results, and career effects remain unknown.

Where could earlier preparation shape the evidence used for a later opportunity?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: This response follows the possible mechanism from early access to later evidence. It connects the selected goals without making identity or familiarity a complete explanation. Appropriate criteria and support remain part of actual employment processes. Guidance can deepen the comparison, but interest, feasibility, individual results, and the lasting effect on opportunity still need evidence from the work.

slides.text:
Workforce goals across the life cycle
In this example, an area connects Hiring and retention, Learning and development, and Eliminating disparities around access to useful preparation and assignments.

Examine recruitment, onboarding, support, development, recognition, and transition where relevant. The same condition can carry forward, but the full effect needs evidence.
slides.narration: The selected goals can reinforce one another through a meaningful opportunity path. Staff need to understand available development and have usable preparation for relevant assignments. Recognition may affect what evidence is available later. Follow those conditions without treating tenure, identity, or one course answer as an assessment of the person. The actual employment processes remain. A work-plan inquiry can identify a repeated opportunity gap and compare support alternatives while keeping individual goals, selection outcomes, and career effects open.

slides.text:
Learning and guidance extend capability
Resources can support substantive understanding, private reflection, and practice in the actual subject. Staff can use them voluntarily and seek guidance when useful.

Learning is part of the plan where it fits the goal. It should not replace examination of a service rule, opportunity route, or other condition that requires action.
slides.narration: A learning resource may help staff understand a service assumption or examine how evidence supports a recommendation. That capability matters in its own right and can support practical work. Yet a presentation alone does not change a rule or create an unavailable support route. Ask what learning contributes to this plan and what other responsibility remains. The consultant can guide that connection without doing everyone’s work. This preserves the program’s aim of growing independent equity practice alongside access to substantive support.

slides.text:
Culture briefs support the inquiry
Use briefs to prepare questions about meaning, communication, and participation. Ask people what matters in the particular service or workplace situation.

A brief cannot select the three goals for a community or predict an individual’s preference. Keep the actual account and the plan’s question central.
slides.narration: A brief can widen the supervisor’s or manager’s preparation by introducing considerations they might overlook. It does not determine what a person wants or which explanation fits an observed difference. The work plan should remain connected to actual accounts and conditions. Repeating a group assumption can make the plan appear culturally informed while missing the practical barrier. A better approach uses the brief to ask more thoughtful questions and preserves different meanings among people who share an identity or community.

slides.text:
Make responsibility understandable
Describe the proposed action and the actual role that can consider or carry it out. Do not assign new authority, workloads, or partner duties from a template.

Where a dependency remains, name the question plainly. Required policy, employment, service, and other processes continue through their responsible roles.
slides.narration: A work-plan entry should help someone understand what needs to happen and which actual responsibility matters. It should not turn a helpful learning suggestion into an assignment for an office that has not agreed or give a supervisor authority outside their role. If another responsibility is needed, explain that dependency and seek the appropriate discussion. Repeated vague ownership can leave work stalled or burden someone unexpectedly. Clear language supports coordination while respecting the real boundaries of the decision and the people involved.

slides.text:
Separate action from intended result
A revised notice, reviewed requirement, or supported learning opportunity is an action or output. Usable clarification or opportunity is an intended result to examine.

Choose evidence that fits the question. Missing experience remains unknown, and an appealing proposal is not a completed outcome.
slides.narration: The distinction helps a plan remain honest about progress. You can describe a prepared change and explain why it may address the condition. Later evidence can examine whether people could use the route or participate in the opportunity. Neither stage should be dismissed, and neither should answer the other’s question. A simple logic model can connect resources, activities, outputs, intended outcomes, and longer-term change without turning the arrows into proof. The plan becomes more useful when those claims are understandable and separate.

slides.text:
Community endorsement in the work-plan update
A participant suggests a clearer question route. The proposed route has not been used. In this example, a progress update says the community approved the plan and disparities were eliminated. What account is supported?
A. The original update because the suggestion was useful.
B. The account informed a proposed route; actual use, wider agreement, and effects remain unexamined through the appropriate review.
C. No progress can be described until every long-term result is known.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The participant’s suggestion has helped develop a proposal, which is meaningful progress. The new route has not been used, and the account does not establish whole-community agreement. A faithful update describes the contribution, the proposed change, the relevant review, and the evidence needed next. A culture brief can prepare further questions without becoming proof of endorsement. Repeated premature achievement claims may hide a condition that still needs attention. The stronger account neither declares the goals achieved nor dismisses the work already done; it keeps the actual stage and intended result understandable.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. The original update because the suggestion was useful.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. The account informed a proposed route; actual use, wider agreement, and effects remain unexamined through the appropriate review.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. No progress can be described until every long-term result is known.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A useful suggestion is not endorsement or a completed result. Repeated claims can hide remaining conditions. Preserve the contribution and proposal, then examine use and effects; community agreement and eliminated disparities are unestablished.

How can the update recognize a useful contribution and preserve what still needs evidence?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The original update changes the contribution into a community verdict and the proposal into an achieved effect. Repetition can make unresolved conditions disappear from the plan. Preserve the particular suggestion and the actual stage of work. The participant did not supply universal approval, the route has not been used, and no evidence of eliminated disparities is supplied in this exercise.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This recognizes progress within its scope. A proposed route may address a recurring gap, but actual use needs evidence. Explain the contribution, review, and open questions; neither wider endorsement nor lasting change is supplied.

How can the update recognize a useful contribution and preserve what still needs evidence?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: This account values the contribution and keeps the plan’s current stage clear. The proposal can be compared with the recurring route question while actual use and effects remain open. Appropriate review and information arrangements still apply. A useful suggestion is not public endorsement by a community, and a proposed route is not a demonstrated lasting change.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Preparation and a supported proposal are meaningful progress. Erasing them can obscure useful work. Describe the current stage and intended effect honestly; long-term results remain unknown without making all progress invisible.

How can the update recognize a useful contribution and preserve what still needs evidence?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: Long-term uncertainty does not make current progress meaningless. The contribution and proposal can be described accurately while keeping intended outcomes separate. Repeated all-or-nothing reporting may hide both useful work and continuing questions. State what is prepared and what still needs examination. The case establishes neither complete success nor the absence of progress, and no timetable or new reporting structure is needed to make that distinction.

slides.text:
A progress account that helps the work
Describe what is prepared, examined, carried out, and still open. Keep the selected goals and relevant evidence connected with the actual question.

The account can fit an existing work plan. This course does not prescribe a timetable, reporting cycle, or a new administrative structure.
slides.narration: A practical account lets a colleague understand the state of the work and what needs an answer. It might distinguish a drafted explanation from an authorized release or an intended improvement from observed use. That precision helps the responsible people respond to a real dependency. The account should fit the existing arrangement rather than create another reporting burden. A useful plan remains specific enough to guide action without inventing the cadence, authority, or commitments that the people involved have not established.

slides.text:
Draft the three-goal connection
Choose a practice or actual question and explain why three goals fit. For each, name the condition, possible action, and evidence question.

Which part requires consultant guidance or another actual responsibility? Keep the proposed plan separate from approval and do not prescribe a date that has not been agreed.
slides.narration: Try the connection in ordinary language. You might explain that a communication goal concerns a usable question route, an engagement goal concerns the account of people affected, and a contract goal concerns an actual response arrangement. Then ask which information or responsibility is still needed. The draft is preparation for discussion, not a finished analysis or an independent authorization. This reflection can use fiction and remain private while helping you distinguish a meaningful goal connection from three labels placed on the same activity.

slides.text:
Respond to an unresolved condition
If a proposed change cannot yet proceed, explain the reason and the relevant next question. Do not hide the gap or invent a decision power to close it.

Consultation can help examine alternatives and recommendations. An actual accommodation, complaint, safety issue, or required review still follows its own process.
slides.narration: A barrier in the plan may concern resources, information, or a responsibility that needs clarification. Naming it is useful work, not a failure of commitment. The consultant can help compare alternatives or strengthen the evidence-supported recommendation. Yet the plan must not absorb an actual request that has its own required response. Keep those responsibilities distinct and dependable. A sustained approach can acknowledge the unresolved condition, preserve support where possible, and identify an appropriate next inquiry without claiming that the issue has been resolved.

slides.text:
Examine actual use and revise thoughtfully
After an action occurs, compare its use and remaining conditions with the original question. Explain changes in scope or context.

Different evidence may support different findings. A narrower gain can be meaningful while broader disparities, trust, or lasting effects remain unestablished.
slides.narration: A revised route may become easier to use while the next explanation remains unclear. That is an informative result because it shows both progress and a continuing question. Compare evidence within its actual scope and recognize other changes that could matter. Avoid making one favorable observation represent all selected goals. The plan can adapt through the existing responsibilities, with guidance where useful. Its seriousness comes from learning about the work as it is, rather than protecting a promised result that the evidence does not support.

slides.text:
Three goals, one meaningful work connection
Select three goals with reasons, examine the actual condition and alternatives, and connect action with evidence and appropriate responsibilities.

The consultant provides guidance as needed. The plan supports useful equity practice without replacing shared understanding, existing processes, or the people who carry out the work.
slides.narration: The three-goal plan can connect a broad equity direction with practical work in a supervisor’s or manager’s area. Its value lies in the reasons, conditions, alternatives, and evidence it makes understandable. You have practiced those connections without inventing a timetable or decision chain. Return to the question that matters in your area and ask where consultation would deepen the analysis. A focused, supported plan can help the work move thoughtfully while keeping intended improvement, actual progress, and unresolved responsibility distinct.

outcomes: Explain the six ADSA goals using the program’s documented wording.
Select three relevant goals and connect each with a real organizational condition.
Examine how the three selected goals reinforce one another or create competing demands across service and workplace conditions, and use relevant evidence to guide follow-through.
Identify where consultation and guidance would help clarify the plan.
